prompt: Version control tracks ___ to your files.
Version control shows when a change happened.
explanation: Every recorded change carries a timestamp of when it happened.

prompt: Which is a real VCS benefit?
Recovering deleted work is hard without version control.
Which are real version-control benefits?
You can see ___ changed a file.
Every Git ___ holds the full project history.
explanation: This is what makes Git "distributed" — there's no single machine that alone holds the real history.

prompt: What's distributed VCS's main advantage?
explanation: Because every developer gets a full copy of the repository, you can commit changes and work entirely without an internet connection until you reconnect.

prompt: A down server blocks Git history access.
explanation: Every clone already has the full history — the server going down blocks sharing, not working.

prompt: Being ___ lets you commit offline.
explanation: Distributed systems give every user a full copy of the repository, meaning you can record changes locally without needing constant server access.

prompt: Git being distributed means no shared version.
explanation: Distributed just means everyone ALSO has a full local copy — teams can still work from one shared copy too.

prompt: Complete: set your Git username globally.
explanation: The correct option to complete the command is `user.name`, which tells Git that you are setting your identity for all future commits on this machine.

prompt: Complete: set your Git email globally.
explanation: The key you are setting here is your user email, which Git recognizes as `user.email`. This tells Git what identity to attach to your commits.

prompt: `--global` applies to every repo, not just one.
explanation: That's right; using `--global` sets configuration variables for your entire user account on your machine, affecting all future repositories you work in.

prompt: What does git config `--global` set?
explanation: It primarily sets user-specific metadata, like your name and email address, which Git uses to identify who made the commit. It doesn't affect file or branch names.

prompt: Which flag makes config apply everywhere?
explanation: The `--global` flag tells Git to save this setting in your user's global configuration file, making it available across all projects on your machine.

prompt: Skip the ___ flag to set locally.
explanation: If you don't specify any scope flag at all, Git assumes you mean the current repository (local) and ignores your system or global settings for this specific project.

prompt: Your name and email attach to every commit.
explanation: Yes, Git requires you to set your name and email so that every commit is properly attributed to a specific user. This ensures a clear history of who made which changes.

prompt: Complete: turn this folder into a repo.
explanation: You must run the full command `git init` to initialize a folder. This action creates the hidden `.git` directory, which is where Git stores all its tracking data.

prompt: Running `git init` deletes any existing files in the folder.
explanation: It only adds Git's own hidden tracking folder — your files are untouched.

prompt: Where does Git store its own tracking data?
explanation: Git keeps all of its internal metadata—including object history and configuration—within the dedicated, hidden `.git` folder inside your project directory. This folder is what makes it a repository.

prompt: You can run `git init` on a non-empty folder.
explanation: True; running `git init` on an existing folder doesn't delete anything but simply sets up the necessary version control structure so that Git can begin tracking all the files already present.

prompt: Which command starts a new empty repo?
explanation: Use `git init` when you want to start tracking a brand new folder locally; it initializes all the necessary Git files for an empty repository.

prompt: Complete: copy a remote repo locally.
explanation: The command needed is clone, as '`git clone` [URL]' downloads the entire history and structure of a remote repository to your local machine.

prompt: `git clone` skips the project's full history.
explanation: A clone brings down the entire history by default, not just a snapshot.

prompt: `git clone` names your remote ___ by default.
explanation: Git automatically names the primary remote connection point—the source you cloned from—as 'origin' for easy reference later on.

prompt: Cloning alone gives you a ready-to-commit copy.
explanation: Yes, cloning downloads the full history and sets up your local branch to point directly at the latest commit, making it ready for immediate work.

prompt: Which command starts a brand-new project?
explanation: `git init` is used when you are starting from scratch in an empty directory; `git clone` only copies a project that already exists somewhere else.

prompt: Version control tracks changes to your files.
explanation: That's exactly right; version control systems record a complete history, allowing you to see who changed what and when.

prompt: Every Git clone stores the full history.
explanation: Yes, when you clone a repository, you get a complete copy of all branches and the entire commit history locally.

prompt: `--global` makes a Git setting global.
explanation: The `--global` flag applies the setting across all repositories on your machine, while using no flag (or `--local`) limits the setting only to the current repository you are working in.

prompt: `git init` turns a folder into a repo.
explanation: Yes, running `git init` in any folder initializes it as a Git repository, allowing you to start tracking changes within that directory.

prompt: `git clone` copies everything in a repository.
explanation: `git clone` copies the entire contents of an existing remote repository, including all files and the full history of commits.

prompt: A staged change is ready to commit.
explanation: That's exactly right; staging is the process of selecting which changes will be included in the next snapshot, making them ready for the commit command.

prompt: Which Git area holds an about-to-save change?
explanation: The Staging Area acts like a waiting room—it’s where you curate and select specific changes from your Working Directory that you want to include in the upcoming commit.

prompt: Editing a file only changes the Working Directory at first.
explanation: Correct. Simply editing a file only affects your local copy (the Working Directory); you must manually tell Git to track it before committing.

prompt: Preparing changes move into the ___.
explanation: This action moves local file changes into the staging area, preparing them for commitment.

prompt: Saving changes moves them into the ___.
explanation: Saving changes takes everything from the staging area and permanently saves it as a snapshot within the repository's history.

prompt: A change must be staged before it can be committed.
explanation: That's correct. Git only commits what you explicitly tell it to track; you must manually prepare those changes before committing.

prompt: Which command moves changes staged?
explanation: This command takes modifications from your working directory and places them into the staging index, preparing it for a save.

prompt: Committing removes the file from the Working Directory.
explanation: The file stays in your Working Directory too — commit just saves a snapshot.

prompt: Order Git's basic save flow.
explanation: First, modify the file. Next, prepare the changes for saving. Finally, save the prepared snapshot.

prompt: Once committed, where does a snapshot permanently live?
explanation: The repository is where Git stores all your permanent history; once committed, that snapshot lives forever in the repo's object database.

prompt: `git add` stages your changes.
explanation: Git add moves changes from your working directory into the staging area, which is like a preparation zone for your next commit.

prompt: Complete: stage a single file.
explanation: You use the syntax `git add` [filename] to specifically tell Git which file you want included in the next snapshot.

prompt: `git add` stages only the file you name.
explanation: That's right; `git add` is very precise. If you run it without specifying a file, it won't stage anything by default.

prompt: `git ___ file.txt` stages one file.
explanation: `add` is the command that moves changes into the staging area, preparing them to be saved in your repository history.

prompt: Which command stages one file?
explanation: The `git add` command is specifically designed for staging files. Remember that saving changes commits them, and checking status just shows you what's going on.

prompt: `git status` shows which files are staged.
explanation: Yes, '`git status`' is the primary command used to see exactly which changes are staged and ready for commit.

prompt: Which command shows staged files?
explanation: '`git status`' shows you the current state of your repository, including what has been added to the staging area. '`git add`' moves files *to* the staging area, and '`git log`' tracks history.

prompt: `git status` changes any files.
explanation: It only reports state — it never modifies your files.

prompt: `git ___` shows what's staged.
explanation: The 'status' command is designed specifically to report on the state of your working directory and staging index, telling you what has been staged.

prompt: `git status` shows unstaged changes too.
explanation: Absolutely. It gives a comprehensive view by showing unstaged changes (in your working directory) alongside staged files.

prompt: `git add` . stages every changed file.
explanation: That's correct; using '`git add` .' is the quick way to stage all modified and new files in the current directory and its subdirectories.

prompt: Complete: stage every changed file.
explanation: To stage all changes in the current directory, you use `git add .` because the dot (`.`) represents everything relative to your current location.

prompt: `git add` . stages just one file.
explanation: The . means every changed file in this folder, not just one.

prompt: Which command stages all changes?
explanation: The command `add `. stages every modified and new file in your repository; using just `add file` only targets a specific file, and `status` only shows what has changed.

prompt: `git add` ___ stages everything.
explanation: `git add .` is the correct syntax because the dot (`.`) tells Git to stage all changes within the current directory structure.

prompt: `-m` adds a commit message.
explanation: The `-m` flag allows you to provide a commit message directly on the command line, whereas `-a` stages modified files and `-v` shows verbose output.

prompt: Complete: commit with a message flag.
explanation: You use `git commit -m` followed by your desired message in quotes; this structure tells Git to perform the commit action while immediately supplying the required message.

prompt: The `-m` flag lets you skip opening an editor.
explanation: Yes, using `-m "message"` lets you provide the commit message right on the command line, bypassing the need for an interactive editor.

prompt: `git commit` ___ adds a message inline.
explanation: You use `-m` to specify a commit message directly on the command line, which is much faster than opening an editor. The `-a` flag stages all modified files, while `-v` just provides verbose output.

prompt: Which flag attaches a message to commit?
explanation: The `-m` flag is specifically designed to allow you to pass a commit message directly as an argument. Flags like `-a` handle file staging, not messaging.

prompt: Commit messages should use the imperative mood.
explanation: This means writing it as if you are giving an instruction, such as "Fix bug X" rather than "Fixed bug X." It makes the commit history read like a set of commands.

prompt: Good commit messages use the ___ mood.
explanation: The imperative mood is best because it frames your commit as a direct instruction to the codebase, like "Add feature X" rather than describing what was done.

prompt: Which is a well-written commit message?
explanation: Good commit messages should be written in the imperative mood, acting like a command. 'Fix login' tells Git what it will do, while 'Fixed bug' is past tense.

prompt: "Fixed the login bug" is imperative mood.
explanation: Imperative mood reads like a command: "Fix", not "Fixed" or "Fixing".

prompt: Write messages in ___ mood, like a command.
explanation: You must write messages using the imperative mood because this style makes your commit message sound like an instruction or command to the codebase.

prompt: `git log` lists commit history.
explanation: The specific Git command used to retrieve and display a record of all commits is `git log`. The other options are incorrect commands.

prompt: Which command lists your commit history?
explanation: You use `git log` to view a complete, chronological list of every commit that has been made in your repository's history.

prompt: `git log` shows the newest commit first.
explanation: Yes, by default, Git displays commits in reverse chronological order, meaning the newest and most recent changes appear at the top of the output.

prompt: What does `git log` NOT show by default?
explanation: Git only tracks history that has already happened, so it cannot show future commits. The author and date are fundamental pieces of information recorded when a commit is made.

prompt: `git ___` lists your commit history.
explanation: The `git log` command is specifically designed to display the full chronological record of your repository's commits. Use `status` to check files and `diff` to see content changes.

prompt: `--oneline` shortens each log entry.
explanation: Using `--oneline` condenses each commit into a single, concise line containing only the abbreviated SHA and message. Remember that `--verbose` actually adds *more* detail, not less.

prompt: Complete: show history, one line each.
explanation: To get a clean, one-line summary of your entire commit history, you must append the `--oneline` flag to the `git log` command.

prompt: `git log --oneline` shows less detail per commit.
explanation: That's correct; the whole purpose of `--oneline` is to strip away extra metadata and condense the output into a single line for quick scanning.

prompt: `git log` ___ shows one line per commit.
explanation: Use `--oneline` because it strips away all the verbose details, showing just the short SHA and the commit message on a single line for quick scanning.

prompt: Why use `git log --oneline`?
explanation: It's perfect for scanning history because it condenses the full commit details into a single line, making it much easier to read than the default output.

prompt: `git diff` shows unstaged changes.
explanation: `git diff` is specifically designed to show the differences between your working files and what Git currently expects, which are your unstaged changes. `git log` shows history, not current file modifications.

prompt: Which command shows unstaged changes?
explanation: The correct command is `git diff`; this utility compares your working directory against the index, revealing everything you haven't staged yet.

prompt: `git diff` shows changes line by line.
explanation: That is correct; `git diff` provides a highly granular, patch-style view that shows exactly which lines were added or removed.

prompt: `git ___` shows unstaged line changes.
explanation: The basic `git diff` command compares your working directory to the staging area, which is exactly where unstaged line changes live. Using `git status` only tells you *if* there are changes, but doesn't show the lines themselves.

prompt: `git diff` compares your files to what?
explanation: By default, `git diff` compares your current working files against what was committed in the last commit (HEAD). If you want to compare it to a different point, like a specific branch or tag, you must specify that reference.

prompt: `--staged` shows only staged changes.
explanation: Using `--staged` tells Git to compare your current files against what you have explicitly added to the staging area (the index). This is useful for checking if everything staged looks correct before committing.

prompt: Complete: diff only staged changes.
explanation: To see only what you've added to the index, you must run `git diff --staged`. This isolates changes that are ready to be committed but haven't been written into the commit history yet.

prompt: `git diff --staged` ignores unstaged changes.
explanation: That is correct; the `--staged` flag specifically compares your working copy to the staging area, completely bypassing any changes you made in your files that you haven't run `git add` on yet.

prompt: `git diff` ___ shows only staged changes.
explanation: Use `git diff --staged` when you only want to see what changes are currently staged for commit, as this compares the staging index against HEAD. Running just '`git diff`' will show unstaged changes in your working directory instead.

prompt: Which shows staged-only changes?
explanation: You must use `git diff --staged` because it specifically compares your staging area (the index) to the last committed state, isolating only what you have added with '`git add`'.

prompt: git restore `--staged` keeps your edits.
explanation: This is true; `git restore --staged` simply moves files out of the staging index back into your working directory without discarding any of the edits you made.

prompt: Complete: unstage a file, keep edits.
explanation: You should use git restore `--staged` <file> because this command specifically removes a file from the staging area while guaranteeing that your actual local changes remain untouched in your working directory.

prompt: git restore `--staged` deletes your edits.
explanation: It only unstages — your edits stay right where they are.

prompt: git restore ___ unstages a file.
explanation: Using `git restore --staged <file>` tells Git to move the content of a file out of the staging index and back into your working copy, which is how you unstage it.

prompt: What stays after unstaging a file?
explanation: Unstaging a file moves your changes from the index back to your working directory, meaning all your local edits are preserved. The commit history or the staging area itself remains completely untouched by this action.

prompt: git restore `file.txt` discards unstaged edits.
explanation: That's right; `git restore` is a destructive command that overwrites your working copy with the contents of a specified commit, discarding any local changes you made since then.

prompt: `git ___ file.txt` discards unstaged edits.
explanation: You need to use `git restore` because it is the modern, dedicated tool for reverting unstaged files back to their committed state. Using `reset` or `diff` will either affect commits or just show differences without discarding anything.

prompt: git restore `file.txt` permanently discards edits.
explanation: This is true because running `git restore` overwrites your local working directory files with the version stored in Git, making those specific edits effectively lost from your current workspace.

prompt: git restore `file.txt` reverts to the last ___.
explanation: `git restore` reverts your file to match the state of the most recent commit, which is its source of truth. It doesn't use branch or remote information when performing this local rollback.

prompt: Which command discards unstaged edits?
explanation: git restore is the command designed to discard uncommitted changes from your working directory back to what Git last tracked. While `git diff` shows you exactly what changed, it does nothing to actually undo those edits.

prompt: `git commit --amend` replaces your last commit.
explanation: That's right; using `--amend` rewrites history by replacing the content of your most recent commit with whatever changes you stage and commit now.

prompt: Complete: fix your most recent commit.
explanation: You need to use `git commit --amend` because this specific flag tells Git that you intend to modify, rather than append to, your previous commit.

prompt: `git commit --amend` creates a brand-new commit.
explanation: It replaces the last commit rather than adding another one.

prompt: `git commit` ___ fixes your last commit.
explanation: The correct option is `--amend`, as it is the dedicated flag used to overwrite or adjust the contents of the most recent commit. The other options are not recognized flags for this action.

prompt: What can `--amend` change?
explanation: `--amend` can update the commit message, the staged changes, or both at once.

prompt: git revert creates a new commit that undoes changes.
explanation: This is accurate; git revert never deletes history, instead creating a new, explicit commit that reverses the changes from a specific point in time, which keeps your log clean and traceable.

prompt: What does git revert do?
explanation: It doesn't delete the commit; instead, it creates a brand new commit that contains the inverse changes of the specified commit. This method is safe because it never rewrites or deletes history.

prompt: git revert removes the original commit from history.
explanation: It leaves the original commit in place and adds a new one that undoes it.

prompt: `git ___` <commit> undoes it with a new commit.
explanation: You use `git revert` because it specifically generates a compensating, new commit to undo the changes without rewriting any existing history. Using `reset` would move your branch pointer and potentially lose commits for everyone else.

prompt: After reverting one commit, how many new commits appear?
explanation: Since `git revert` is designed to undo changes by creating a single corrective patch, it will always introduce exactly one new commit object into your history.

prompt: Revert is safer than reset after pushing.
explanation: This is true because `git revert` only adds commits, maintaining the historical record that everyone else has already pulled. Using `reset` after pushing would rewrite shared history and cause major problems for your teammates.

prompt: A teammate already pulled a bad commit. Safe fix?
explanation: You must use `git revert` because it creates a new compensating commit that undoes the damage without altering any of the shared history your teammate has already pulled. Using `reset` would rewrite history and break their local repository.

prompt: `git reset --hard` is safe on commits others already pulled.
explanation: It rewrites history, which breaks teammates' copies of the branch.

prompt: ___ is safe for shared history, not rewriting.
explanation: Revert is safe for shared history because it creates a brand new commit that undoes the changes of a previous one, leaving the original history intact. Resetting or rebasing rewrite history by moving pointers, which should be avoided on public branches.

prompt: Why is git revert safe for pushed commits?
explanation: Revert is safe because it works by creating a new commit that undoes the changes, effectively adding to the history rather than rewriting or deleting commits. This non-destructive approach makes it ideal for shared branches.

prompt: `git reset` moves your branch pointer back.
explanation: This is true; `git reset` fundamentally moves your local branch's HEAD pointer back in time, allowing you to point it at any previous commit hash.

prompt: What does `git reset` move?
explanation: Git reset changes the location of your local branch pointer (the HEAD), moving it backward or forward through history. It does not affect the remote repository or file names directly.

prompt: `git reset` can move your branch to an earlier commit.
explanation: Yes, that is exactly what `git reset` allows you to do; you can move your branch pointer and working directory back to any previous commit in history.

prompt: `git ___` <commit> rewinds the current branch to it.
explanation: Use '`git reset`' with a commit hash when you want to move your branch pointer back in time; 'revert' just creates a new commit that undoes changes without moving history.

prompt: After `git reset`, what happens to later commits?
explanation: They still exist briefly and can often be recovered via the reflog, but your branch no longer points at them.

prompt: `--hard` deletes changes entirely.
explanation: The `--hard` flag is dangerous because it not only moves the branch but also wipes out any uncommitted work and unstaged files entirely.

prompt: Which reset mode deletes your uncommitted changes?
explanation: Using `--hard` deletes everything—the commit history, staged changes, and working directory files—so stick to `--soft` or `--mixed` if you want to keep your work.

prompt: `git reset --mixed` is the default mode.
explanation: That's right; '`git reset --mixed`' is the default behavior when you don't specify a mode, which unstages changes but keeps them in your working directory.

prompt: `git reset` ___ keeps changes staged, ready to commit.
explanation: The `--soft` flag moves the branch pointer back while keeping all files and staged changes exactly as they were before the reset.

prompt: Which mode unstages changes but keeps your files?
explanation: `--soft` keeps changes staged; `--mixed` (the default) unstages them but leaves your files as they are.

prompt: A branch is a movable label, not a copy.
explanation: This is true because branches are merely lightweight pointers that reference a specific commit hash; they do not duplicate the actual files or history.

prompt: What is a Git branch, really?
explanation: A branch is essentially just a movable label pointing to your current commit, which makes it incredibly efficient because Git isn't copying anything when you create one.

prompt: A branch copies all your project files.
explanation: It just points at a commit, so the files belong to the commit, not the branch.

prompt: A branch points at one ___.
explanation: Branches always point specifically at a single commit hash. This commit represents the complete snapshot of all files and changes that occurred at that moment in time.

prompt: What happens to a branch label after a commit?
explanation: When you successfully make a new commit, Git automatically updates the branch label to point directly at that brand-new commit hash, causing it to move forward along the history line.

prompt: Creating a branch does not switch to it.
Complete: create a branch called feature.
explanation: The correct syntax requires the word 'branch' immediately after `git` and before the name you want. So, the full command is `git branch feature`. It was an older command used to switch between branches or restore files.

prompt: `git branch` feature switches you onto feature.
explanation: It only creates the label; you stay on your current branch until you switch.

prompt: `git ___` <name> creates a new branch.
explanation: The '`git branch` <name>' command simply creates the pointer to a new branch, but you need 'git switch' or '`git checkout`' to actually move your working directory onto it.

prompt: Where does a new branch initially point?
explanation: When you create a new branch, it is initially set up to point exactly at the commit where you ran the command (the current HEAD).

prompt: git switch moves you onto another branch.
explanation: That's right; 'git switch' is specifically designed to change your active branch and update your working files accordingly.

prompt: Complete: move onto the feature branch.
explanation: You need to use 'git switch' followed by the name of the branch you want to move onto, like this: git switch feature

prompt: Switching branches updates your working files.
explanation: Yes, switching branches is designed to update your local working directory and files so they reflect the state of that new branch.

prompt: `git ___` moves you onto an existing branch.
explanation: Use `git switch` when you just want to jump between branches without creating new ones; it's the modern command designed specifically for this purpose.

prompt: What is the older command for switching branches?
explanation: Before Git introduced dedicated commands like `switch`, you had to use `git checkout` to switch branches or restore files, making it the older utility.

prompt: `-c` creates and switches branches at once.
explanation: The `-c` flag tells Git to create the branch *and* immediately switch your working directory to it, saving you a second command.

prompt: Complete: create and switch to feature.
explanation: You need to include the `-c` flag right after `switch` so Git knows you want to create a new branch named 'feature' immediately and move to it.

prompt: git switch `-c` both creates and switches in one step.
explanation: That is correct; the `-c` flag handles the entire process, creating the branch and moving you to it in a single command.

prompt: `git checkout` ___ works the same as switch `-c`.
explanation: The correct option, `-b`, tells git to create a new branch and immediately check it out. This functionality is exactly what `git switch -c` does.

prompt: `git merge` combines another branch into yours.
explanation: This is correct; merging takes all the commits and history from the source branch and integrates them into your current working branch.

prompt: Complete: merge feature into your current branch.
explanation: You need to specify the source branch name, so you run `git merge feature`. This tells Git exactly which set of changes you want to integrate into your current location.

prompt: `git merge` combines two branches into one history.
explanation: That's right; the entire point of merging is to combine two separate histories into one cohesive timeline, resulting in a merge commit.

prompt: `git ___` <branch> brings its commits into yours.
Which branch do you merge into?
explanation: You always perform a merge *into* your current branch, as that is the target location where all incoming changes will be applied.

prompt: Fast-forward merge happens when nothing has diverged.
explanation: That's correct; a fast-forward merge only happens when the history of one branch hasn't diverged from the other, so no complex merging logic is needed.

prompt: When does Git do a fast-forward merge?
explanation: A fast-forward merge occurs when one branch is simply ahead of the other and their histories haven't branched apart yet. If they have diverged, a full merge commit is required.

prompt: A fast-forward merge creates a new merge commit.
explanation: It just moves the pointer forward since there is nothing to combine.

prompt: A ___ merge just moves your pointer forward.
explanation: A fast-forward merge doesn't require combining changes; it just moves the target branch's pointer forward to match the source, keeping history linear and avoiding a dedicated merge commit.

prompt: What does a fast-forward merge require?
explanation: If your branch has commits the other doesn't, Git can't just move the pointer — it needs a real merge commit instead.

prompt: A three-way merge commit has two parents.
explanation: That is correct. A standard merge commit must record two parents because it is explicitly combining changes from two separate lines of development.

prompt: How many parents does a three-way merge commit have?
explanation: A merge commit always has at least two parents—the tips of the branches being merged. Since a three-way merge is just a specific type of merge, it retains those two parent pointers.

prompt: A three-way merge happens when both branches diverged.
explanation: Exactly; a three-way merge requires finding the common ancestor point where the two lines of development split off.

prompt: A merge commit has two ___.
explanation: Merge commits are defined by having multiple parent pointers, which track the history of the converging branches.

prompt: What does a three-way merge combine?
explanation: It's designed to integrate changes from two separate, diverging lines of development back into a single cohesive history.

prompt: A merge conflict means both branches changed one line.
explanation: Yes, a conflict occurs when Git cannot automatically determine which change to keep because two different branches modified the exact same lines of code.

prompt: What causes a merge conflict?
explanation: A conflict only occurs when Git finds that two separate branches modified the exact same lines of code differently. A typo or adding a new file won't trigger this specific type of merge conflict.

prompt: Git resolves every merge conflict automatically.
explanation: Conflicting lines need a human decision, so Git pauses and asks you to fix them.

prompt: Git marks conflicts with <<<<<<< and ___.
explanation: The markers use `<<<<<<<` to show your local changes, and they use `>>>>>>>` to mark the end of the incoming changes from the other branch. This structure helps you see exactly where the code diverged.

prompt: After fixing a conflict, what do you do next?
explanation: Staging the resolved file and committing it is what tells Git the conflict is settled.

prompt: `git rebase` replays your commits on another branch.
explanation: That's right; rebase is powerful because it takes all of your commits and reapplies them one by one onto a new base branch. This effectively rewrites history to make it look like you started from that other point.

prompt: Complete: replay your commits on top of main.
explanation: To replay your changes on top of main, you run `git rebase main` while checked out on your feature branch. You are telling Git to take all commits from your current branch and place them sequentially after the latest commit in main.

prompt: Rebasing creates a merge commit like `git merge` does.
explanation: It replays your commits one by one for a straight line of history instead.

prompt: `git ___` replays commits on top of another branch.
explanation: Rebase literally replays your commits one by one on top of the target branch, making it look like they were always there. Merge combines histories using a special commit, while revert simply undoes changes.

prompt: What kind of history does rebasing produce?
explanation: Since rebase reapplies your commits sequentially onto the new base, it creates a perfectly clean and linear history. A merge commit is what introduces the non-linear 'forked' look.

prompt: `git rebase -i` lets you edit past commits.
explanation: That's correct; interactive rebase is specifically designed for rewriting history, which includes editing or amending past commits. This power requires caution, though!

prompt: What does `git rebase -i` let you do?
explanation: The `-i` flag opens up a powerful interface that lets you rewrite and polish your commit history by squashing, dropping, or amending old changes.

prompt: Interactive rebase can combine several commits into one.
explanation: Yes, that's exactly what it does; you use `git rebase -i` to pick and choose which commits get combined or edited before they are finalized.

prompt: `git rebase` ___ opens the interactive commit list.
explanation: You need the `-i` flag (for interactive) because it tells Git to open the special editor that lets you review and manipulate the commit history list.

prompt: Combining several commits into one is called what?
explanation: While rebasing involves rewriting history, the specific action of combining multiple commits into a single unit is called squashing.

prompt: A Git remote is a linked repository.
explanation: Correct; think of it as a pointer to another repository (like on GitHub) that allows you to push and pull changes between machines.

prompt: What is a remote in Git?
explanation: A remote refers to an external repository location, essentially a linked copy that allows you to collaborate with others over networks.

prompt: The default remote name is origin.
Git names the default remote ___.
Where does a remote usually live?
`git push` sends local commits to a remote.
Which command sends your commits to a remote?
`git pull` brings remote commits into your branch.
`git ___` sends your local commits to the remote.
explanation: You use `git push` when you want to send your completed local commits up to the shared remote server. Git pull is used for downloading changes from others.

prompt: What does `git pull` do after downloading?
explanation: Git pull first downloads the remote changes, and then it automatically attempts to merge those new commits into your current local branch.

prompt: `git fetch` downloads commits without changing your branch.
explanation: That's right; fetch only downloads information about what others have done without affecting your current local code or pointer.

prompt: What does `git fetch` do to your branch?
explanation: Git fetch simply downloads data into your repository without making any changes or updating your actual working branch pointer.

prompt: `git pull` automatically merges after downloading.
explanation: Yes, that's exactly what it does; 'pull' is a convenient shortcut that combines downloading (fetching) and integrating those changes (merging).

prompt: `git ___` downloads without touching your branch.
explanation: Fetch is designed to download all remote changes and store them locally without applying or merging anything, keeping your current branch safe. Pull, on the other hand, performs both the fetch and the merge automatically.

prompt: Which is the safer, quieter option: fetch or pull?
explanation: Fetch is safer because it only downloads data into your repository's remote tracking branches, leaving your working local branches completely untouched. Pull combines fetching with merging, which can sometimes introduce unexpected changes or conflicts.

prompt: A tracking branch remembers its matching remote branch.
explanation: That's exactly what a tracking branch does; it establishes a permanent link to its counterpart on a remote repository. This linkage is key because it allows Git to manage synchronization automatically.

prompt: What does a tracking branch remember?
explanation: A tracking branch's main job is maintaining awareness of its corresponding remote branch, which dictates where it should look for updates. It has nothing to do with the color or author of the code.

prompt: A tracking branch lets push/pull skip naming the remote.
explanation: Since a tracking branch already knows exactly which remote and branch it belongs to, Git automatically uses that information when you run pull or push. You don't need to specify the destination every time.

prompt: A ___ branch is linked to one remote branch.
explanation: A tracking branch is specifically designed to monitor and sync with one particular remote branch, giving you clear visibility into where your local code stands relative to the server.

prompt: Why is a tracking branch useful?
explanation: It saves typing because a tracking branch automatically knows which remote repository it corresponds to, so you don't have to specify that name every time you pull or push.

prompt: A fork is your own copy of a repo.
explanation: That is correct; a fork creates an entirely separate, personal copy of someone else's repository under your own account for independent work.

prompt: What is a GitHub fork?
explanation: A GitHub fork is an independent, full replica of the entire repository that lives under your user profile, which is different from simply creating a branch within the original repo. It is a mechanism for proposing changes to a project's main codebase.

prompt: A pull request asks to merge your changes.
explanation: That's right; it’s the formal process you use to propose that your work from one branch should be reviewed and integrated into another, like merging into main.

prompt: A ___ is your hosted copy of a repo.
explanation: A fork creates your own independent copy of a repository under your account, allowing you to experiment without affecting the original.

prompt: What does a pull request let a maintainer do?
explanation: Pull requests are designed specifically for maintainers to review proposed changes from contributors before they are merged into the main codebase.

prompt: Small, focused commits are easier to review.
explanation: Yes, small commits that address one specific change make it much easier for others to understand and approve your work.

prompt: What makes a commit easy to review?
explanation: Small, focused changes are ideal because reviewers can quickly grasp the purpose of the commit without getting lost in unrelated code modifications.

prompt: One giant commit mixing several changes is easy to review.
explanation: Reviewers have to untangle unrelated changes, which slows everything down.

prompt: Keep each commit ___ and small.
explanation: Commits should be focused so that each one represents a single, logical change or feature addition.

prompt: Why write an honest commit message?
explanation: Writing honest commit messages provides context for reviewers, allowing them to understand the 'why' behind a change rather than just the 'what.' This makes code review much faster and more effective.

prompt: Trunk-based development merges tiny changes constantly.
explanation: That’s right; trunk-based development is defined by integrating small changes into the main branch continuously. This prevents large, painful merges later on.

prompt: Which strategy merges tiny changes into main constantly?
explanation: Trunk-based development is the strategy that requires developers to merge tiny changes into the main line constantly. Git Flow and Forking are much more structured or isolated in their merging practices.

prompt: Git Flow uses long-lived branches for scheduled releases.
explanation: That’s correct; Git Flow relies on dedicated, long-lived branches for releases, which is its defining characteristic compared to continuous integration models.

prompt: A ___ branch isolates one change at a time.
explanation: A feature branch is specifically designed to isolate a single piece of work so that it doesn't break the main codebase while you are developing it.

prompt: What is a feature branch used for?
explanation: A feature branch is used to isolate a single change or new function so you can develop it without risking the stability of your main codebase.

prompt: A .gitignore file excludes files from tracking.
What does a .gitignore file do?
Secrets belong in .gitignore, not in a commit.
explanation: If you commit secrets, they are permanently recorded in Git's history, making them impossible to truly delete. They must be listed in .gitignore instead.

prompt: Git reads ignore patterns from ___.
explanation: The specific file that tells Git which files or patterns to ignore is always named .gitignore, keeping your repository clean and focused on source code.

prompt: What is a common thing to ignore?
explanation: Build output (like compiled binaries) should be ignored because they are generated every time you compile the project and aren't part of the actual source code that needs version control.

prompt: git clean `-f` deletes only untracked files.
explanation: That is correct; git clean only targets untracked files, which means it won't touch any files Git is already managing or tracking.

prompt: What does git clean `-f` delete?
explanation: The `-f` flag stands for force, which is necessary because `git clean` defaults to being safe and won't delete anything unless you explicitly force it. It specifically targets untracked files in your working directory.

prompt: git clean `-n` previews without deleting anything.
explanation: That's correct; the `-n` flag (or `--dry-run`) is exactly what you need to see which files *would* be deleted without actually removing them from your disk.

prompt: git clean ___ previews what would be deleted.
explanation: You need `-n` because it tells Git to run a dry run, showing you the list of potential deletions without making any actual changes. Using `-f` would force the deletion immediately.

prompt: Does git clean touch tracked files?
explanation: No, `git clean` is designed only for untracked files; it will never touch or delete anything that Git already knows about and tracks in your repository.

prompt: `git log -S` finds commits touching that text.
explanation: Yes, `-S` stands for 'pickaxe' mode, meaning it searches the commit history specifically by looking at changes to content (the diff), rather than just checking if a file was modified.

prompt: Complete: find commits mentioning TODO.
explanation: To search for text within commit messages specifically, you need to use the `--grep` flag; simply appending the text won't filter by message content.

prompt: `git log -S` finds commits that added or removed text.
explanation: This is correct because the `-S` flag filters commits based on whether they changed the actual content of a specific string, not just if that string was mentioned in the commit message.

prompt: `git log` ___<text> searches commit changes for it.
explanation: You must use `-S` because it performs a content-sensitive search, meaning it only shows commits where the specified text was actually added or removed from the file contents.

prompt: Why use `git log -S` instead of scrolling?
explanation: Using `git log -S` allows you to instantly filter through potentially hundreds of commits, giving you a precise and fast view without manually scrolling.

prompt: git blame shows the last commit per line.
explanation: That's right; it analyzes every single line in a file and tells you exactly which commit introduced that specific piece of code.

prompt: What does git blame show per line?
explanation: It shows the SHA of the commit that last modified that specific line of code. This is useful for understanding history and is distinct from general metrics like file size or branch name.

prompt: git blame is meant to find context, not to accuse.
explanation: That's right; while the name sounds accusatory, it is really just a historical tool designed to help you understand context by showing where lines originated.

prompt: `git ___` <file> shows who last touched each line.
explanation: You need `git blame` because it is specifically designed to map out the authorship and commit details for every single line in a given file. Log gives summaries, while diff compares versions.

prompt: What does git blame operate on?
explanation: It operates at the most granular level by analyzing each individual line of code to determine its history and origin within the repository.

prompt: git bisect helps find the commit that broke something.
explanation: That's exactly what it does; `bisect` uses a binary search process across your commit history to quickly narrow down the exact commit that introduced a bug.

prompt: What does git bisect find?
explanation: Git bisect uses a binary search approach to efficiently narrow down the exact commit that introduced a bug, rather than just finding a branch or remote location.

prompt: git bisect needs a known-good and known-bad commit.
explanation: Yes, you must tell `git bisect` where to start by providing at least one known-good and one known-bad commit so it has a range to search within.

prompt: `git ___` narrows down the exact broken commit.
explanation: Bisect is specifically designed to perform a binary search through history, pinpointing the exact commit that caused an issue; blame only tells you who wrote a specific line of code.

prompt: How does git bisect narrow the search?
explanation: Testing the midpoint between a known-good and known-bad commit halves the search space each time.

prompt: `git tag` marks a commit with a name.
explanation: That's correct; tags are essentially permanent, human-readable labels that you attach to specific commits, usually marking releases or milestones.

prompt: Complete: tag the current commit as v2.0.
explanation: To tag your current commit, you simply need to follow `git tag` with the desired version name, like v2.0.

prompt: A tag marks one specific commit permanently.
explanation: That's correct; a tag is an immutable pointer that permanently marks one specific commit in your repository's history.

prompt: `git ___` <name> marks a commit as a release.
explanation: You need to use `git tag` because it creates a permanent, labeled reference point for a commit, which is exactly what you want when marking a release.

prompt: What is a tag typically used for?
explanation: Tags are specifically designed to mark significant milestones in your project's history, making them the standard way to label official releases.

prompt: `git stash` sets aside your uncommitted changes.
explanation: Exactly. `git stash` is perfect for temporarily saving uncommitted work so you can switch contexts without having to commit incomplete changes first.

prompt: What does `git stash` do?
explanation: Git stash takes your uncommitted changes and shelves them temporarily so you can switch branches cleanly. It simply sets the work aside for later use, rather than deleting it or forcing a commit.

prompt: `git stash` pop brings your stashed changes back.
explanation: That's right; `git stash pop` restores your most recent set-aside changes and removes that entry from the stash list simultaneously.

prompt: `git stash` ___ restores your set-aside changes.
explanation: You use `git stash pop` because it not only restores your saved work but also automatically cleans up by removing that entry from the stash stack afterward.

prompt: Why stash before switching branches?
explanation: Git blocks a branch switch when uncommitted changes would conflict with the branch you're moving to.

prompt: git cherry-pick copies just one commit.
explanation: That's correct; `git cherry-pick` is specifically designed to take a single, isolated commit from one branch and apply it onto your current location without bringing over its entire history.

prompt: `git ___` <commit> copies just one commit.
explanation: Cherry-pick is specifically designed to take a single commit from one branch and apply it to your current location. Merging combines entire branches, while rebasing rewrites history by moving commits sequentially.

prompt: Cherry-picking brings the whole branch, not just one commit.
explanation: It copies only the one commit you name, nothing else from that branch.

prompt: One bugfix commit lives elsewhere. Which command?
explanation: `git cherry-pick` copies a single commit onto your branch.

prompt: How many commits does cherry-pick copy?
explanation: By definition, cherry-pick only copies the changes from a single specified commit. It is designed for surgical precision and will not copy an entire history of commits.

prompt: force-with-lease is safer than plain force push.
explanation: It is safer because force-with-lease checks if the remote branch has received any updates since you last pulled, preventing you from accidentally overwriting someone else's work. Plain force push will overwrite regardless of what happened in the meantime.

prompt: Which force-push option is safer?
explanation: Using `--force-with-lease` is safer because it verifies that the remote branch hasn't been updated by anyone else since your local copy was last synchronized, preventing you from accidentally deleting their work.

prompt: You should rewrite commits others already pulled.
explanation: It breaks their local history, so only rewrite commits nobody else has yet.

prompt: `git push` `--force-with-___` is the safer option.
explanation: Using `--force-with-lease` is safer because it checks if the remote branch has been updated by someone else since you last fetched, preventing you from accidentally overwriting their work.

prompt: What does `--force-with-lease` check first?
explanation: It checks nobody else has pushed to the branch since you last fetched, refusing to overwrite their work.

prompt: git reflog records everywhere your branches pointed.
explanation: That's right; the reflog is a comprehensive record that tracks where your local repository's pointers have been moved over time, regardless of which branch you are currently on.

prompt: What does git reflog record?
explanation: It records the movement of your local pointers—essentially a detailed log of every time your branch heads or HEAD itself has been moved or reset.

prompt: The reflog can help recover a commit lost by reset.
explanation: Absolutely; even if a commit is removed from your branch history via a hard reset, the reflog keeps a record of that pointer, making it recoverable.

prompt: `git ___` shows where your branches used to point.
explanation: You need git reflog because it is specifically designed to track every historical movement of your local pointers, showing where branches have been since they were created or moved.

prompt: Why is the reflog called a safety net?
explanation: The reflog tracks every change to your references, essentially creating an audit trail that lets you recover from accidental resets or bad commits.

prompt: Most everyday Git mistakes have simple fixes.
explanation: Yes, Git is designed with powerful safety mechanisms and simple commands to undo most common mistakes without losing data.

prompt: Most everyday Git mistakes have calm, known ___.
explanation: Most everyday Git mistakes have calm, known fixes, meaning you don't need to panic when something goes wrong.

prompt: Wrong-branch commits are what kind of problem?
explanation: Wrong-branch commits are very common and usually easy to fix using commands like `git reset` or `git cherry-pick`.

prompt: A bad commit message is a ___ mistake.
explanation: A bad commit message is a common mistake because it's often overlooked, even though it can make collaboration difficult.

prompt: Forgetting a file in a commit means starting over.
explanation: You can add the file and amend the commit instead of starting over.

prompt: A submodule locks in one exact commit.
explanation: Yes, that's the whole point; when you add a submodule, it locks your parent repository to reference one specific commit from the sub-repository.

prompt: What does a submodule track in the parent repo?
explanation: It only tracks the specific commit hash of the submodule, not every single commit it has ever made. This keeps the parent repo lightweight and stable.

prompt: A submodule is a whole separate repository inside another.
explanation: That's correct; think of it like linking to a separate Git repository that lives inside your main project structure.

prompt: A ___ embeds one repo inside another.
explanation: A submodule is designed specifically to embed one entire, external repository into another existing one.

prompt: Why is a submodule trickier than a normal folder?
explanation: Because the submodule has its own complete history and needs to be managed as a separate Git entity, it's much more complex than just adding a regular folder.

prompt: Git LFS replaces big files with a pointer.
explanation: Yes, that's exactly how it works; instead of storing the huge binary data in Git history, LFS commits only store a tiny pointer to where the actual file lives.

prompt: What does Git LFS replace a large file with?
explanation: It replaces the actual content with a small text file that acts as a reference or pointer, telling Git where to find the large object later on without bloating the repository.

prompt: Git normally struggles with huge binary files.
explanation: Because Git is optimized for tracking source code changes, committing massive binaries bloats the repository history and slows down operations significantly.

prompt: Git ___ keeps large files out of normal history.
explanation: Git LFS was built specifically to manage and track large binary assets, keeping them out of the main repository history where they would cause unnecessary bloat.

prompt: What kind of file is a good LFS candidate?
explanation: Any large, non-textual asset like videos or datasets are perfect candidates because they are big and shouldn't be tracked as plain code changes.

prompt: A Git blob stores a file's contents.
explanation: Yes, a blob is simply a pointer to the raw binary data of a file; it doesn't care about filenames or directory structure.

prompt: In Git's object model what does a blob store?
explanation: A blob stores the actual content of a file—the raw data payload—while tree objects are responsible for organizing that content into directories.

prompt: A tree object holds folder structure.
explanation: That's correct; a tree object maps names to other objects (like blobs or sub-trees), effectively defining the directory layout.

prompt: A commit points at a tree plus its ___.
explanation: A commit needs to know what came before it, so it always points to one or more parent commits in addition to the root tree.

prompt: Which object stores a file's actual content?
explanation: Only the blob object stores the raw data payload; trees organize files into directories, and commits record snapshots over time.

prompt: How many commands does git switch `-c` use?
explanation: It uses only one command because the `-c` flag tells git to create a new branch and simultaneously move you to it, combining two actions into one step.

prompt: `git init` creates a hidden ___ folder.
explanation: It creates a hidden folder named .git; this is where Git stores all its metadata, configuration, and object database for tracking changes.

prompt: `git init` creates a hidden .git folder.
explanation: True. The primary function of `git init` is to create the necessary hidden .git directory structure that defines the current folder as a repository.

prompt: `git init` leaves your existing files ___.
explanation: It leaves your existing files untouched; Git simply starts monitoring them without deleting or altering anything initially.

prompt: `git init` never touches your existing files.
explanation: This is true because `git init` simply sets up the internal tracking system; it doesn't modify or delete any of your actual project files in the current directory.

prompt: The .git folder is hidden by default.
explanation: Yes, the entire repository history and configuration are stored inside this directory, which most operating systems automatically treat as hidden files.

prompt: What does `git init` create?
explanation: It creates the hidden `.git` folder, which is where Git stores all its internal tracking information, history, and configuration files for the repository.

prompt: `git init` is ___ on an existing project.
explanation: It is safe to run; while it creates the `.git` folder, it doesn't alter or delete any of your actual project source code or working files.

prompt: `git init` works inside an existing folder.
explanation: You run it in the folder you want to turn into a repository.

prompt: `git ___` starts a new repository.
explanation: You use `git init` when you want Git to start tracking a brand new project in your current folder, creating the necessary repository files.

prompt: Order how you resolve a merge conflict.
options: Edit the conflicted file|git add|git commit
explanation: You must first manually edit the conflicted file, removing all conflict markers and leaving only the correct code. After resolving it, use `git add` to stage your clean version, and finally, commit the merge using `git commit`.

prompt: Order a git bisect session.
options: git bisect start|git bisect bad|git bisect good
explanation: You must first run git bisect start to initiate the process, followed by defining your initial known-bad and known-good commits to establish the search boundaries.

prompt: Order a stash-and-switch-back workflow.
options: git stash|Handle the urgent task|git stash pop
explanation: The correct order is: first, you `git stash` to save your current changes; next, you switch branches and handle the task; finally, you use `git stash pop` to reapply those saved changes.

prompt: Order replaying your branch on top of main.
explanation: First, switch to your feature branch (`git switch feature`), and then run `git rebase main` from there to replay those commits cleanly on top of the latest changes in main.

prompt: `git status` also shows the current ___.
explanation: `git status` starts by naming the branch you are on.

prompt: `git revert` creates a new ___.
explanation: Revert adds a commit that undoes an earlier one, keeping history intact.

prompt: Which reset mode discards file edits?
explanation: `--hard` resets the files too; `--soft` and `--mixed` keep your edits.

prompt: Interactive rebase can reorder commits.
explanation: In the `-i` list you can move commit lines to change their order.

prompt: A remote is a copy of your repository elsewhere.
explanation: It usually lives on a server such as GitHub.

prompt: Where does a remote usually live?
explanation: A remote is a version of your repository somewhere else, often on GitHub.

prompt: You push commits to a ___.
explanation: Pushing sends your commits to the remote.

prompt: You can pull commits from a remote.
explanation: A remote works both ways: push to it and pull from it.

prompt: Which is an example of a remote?
explanation: GitHub hosts repositories that act as remotes.

prompt: This recap revisits distributed.
explanation: Right: distributed means full history everywhere, and the cards that follow revisit it with other terms.

options: distributed↔Full history everywhere|git config↔Sets Git settings|imperative mood↔Commands, not descriptions|git commit --amend↔Replace last commit
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.

prompt: Pair every term with its gloss.
options: fast-forward merge↔Pointer just moves|three-way merge↔Both branches diverged|merge conflict↔Same lines changed|interactive rebase↔Edit commit list
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.

prompt: Which meaning fits each term?
options: interactive rebase↔Edit commit list|squashing↔Combine commits|tracking branch↔Linked to remote|fork↔Your hosted copy
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.

prompt: Connect the terms to what they mean.
options: pull request↔Ask to merge|trunk-based development↔Small frequent merges|Git Flow↔Release-branch strategy|git clean↔Deletes untracked files
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.

prompt: Match the terms and meanings.
options: git clean↔Deletes untracked files|git log -S↔Search changed text|git blame↔Who changed lines|git bisect↔Binary-search for bug
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.

prompt: Link every term to its idea.
options: git tag↔Names a commit|git stash↔Sets changes aside|git reflog↔Local movement log|submodule↔Repo inside repo
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.

prompt: What does each term mean?
options: submodule↔Repo inside repo|Git LFS↔Large file storage|blob↔Stores file contents|tree object↔Stores folder structure
explanation: Each term is paired with its plain-language meaning.
